title: Dictionaries
subtitle: Stat Sheets and Spell Books
martuIntro:
A list remembers order. It does not remember *meaning*. A [[dictionary]] keeps a tag on every value, and Python calls the tag a key.
In `["Lucky", 13, 26, 3]`, which number is Lucky's armor? Which is his mana? At the Institute, every student had a record with a tag on every line. Mine said *talks too little*.
You have seen dictionaries already: the spell book, the mana bars, and `caster["abilities"]["magical_affinity"]` when you held the barrier. A lot of that code felt like a wall, yes? Tonight we read it one key at a time.
goals: Make a dictionary: a key in quotes, a colon and a value on each line, and say why keys get quotes when variable names don't
Read a value by its key, and fix a KeyError caused by spelling, capitals or a skipped level
Change a value by its key, like spending a hero's mana, and add a new key
Ask whether a key is in a dictionary with `in` and `not in`
Use a key kept in a variable, and know when a key needs quotes
Read and change a value in a dictionary inside a dictionary
Read from a list of dictionaries: the position first, then the key
Build a spell from variables and store it in a spell book under its name
Read a value, compare it, and act on it with `if`, `elif` and `else`, the way the barrier spell did

questions.explain: Read it like a theater ticket: the row first, then the seat. `roster[1]` is row 1, counting from 0: `["Gearshift", 20]`. Then `[1]` is position 1 in that row: 20.

The call hands over 9, so inside the recipe `affinity` is 9. `total` gets `9 * 2`, which is 18, and `return` hands 18 back to the `print`. With no `return`, nothing would come back, and `print` would show `None`.

items.title: Stat Sheets
items.summary: Make stat sheets with dictionaries. Read and change values by their keys, fix KeyErrors, ask `in` and `not in`, and use a key kept in a variable.

exercises.title: Which number is which?
exercises.martu:
A [[list]] remembers order. It doesn't remember *meaning*. In math class, a table of numbers with no column headings is hard to read: is 26 an age or a score? `lucky = ["Lucky", 13, 26, 3]` is like that.
Line 3 keeps Lucky as a list: his name, his magical affinity (how strong his magic is), his max mana (the most magic power he can hold) and his armor bonus, in that order. The notes on lines 1 and 2 say so.
Change the `print` to show his armor bonus. Which position is it? Positions count from 0, like a ruler, yes?

anotherWay.label: Positions under the list
anotherWay.text:
Each item has a position, counting from 0:
```text
["Lucky", 13, 26, 3]
    0     1   2  3
```
Nothing in the list says which number is armor. Only the order does.

anotherWay.label: Lockers with no name tags
anotherWay.text: Picture a row of lockers with no name tags. You have to remember that locker 3 holds the armor. Forget once, and you grab the wrong thing.
My chalk wall is a good list, because its order is its meaning: oldest gap first. A hero's numbers aren't like that. Each one means something different.
Count from 0: name 0, affinity 1, max mana 2, armor 3.

checkpoints.text: On line 4, change the position in `print(lucky[2])` so the line shows Lucky's armor bonus. Positions count from 0.
hints: Look at the notes on lines 1 and 2, then at the list on line 3. Count the items from 0: `"Lucky"` is at position 0. At which position is the armor bonus?
Positions count from 0, like a ruler. In `drill = ["Run", 12, 9]`, `drill[0]` is `"Run"` and `drill[2]` is 9, the third item.
Write `print(lucky[3])` in place of `print(lucky[2])`.

exercises.title: Make a sheet
exercises.martu:
A [[dictionary]] keeps a tag on every value. Python calls the tag a [[key]]. It's like a textbook's glossary: you look up a word, not entry number 3. In `{"mana": 26}`, the key `"mana"` holds 26. I call a dictionary a *sheet*.
Curly braces `{ }` hold the sheet. Each line inside is a key in quotes, a colon, its value and a comma. Read the Example: Bomb Shell's sheet. It prints 6.
Why do keys get quotes? A variable's name never has them: `mana = 26`. A key is text, so it does: `"mana": 26`. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label. *Box* here means a variable, like `mana = 26`. A key is never a box.
Gearshift's sheet. Copy the keys exactly:
```text
GEARSHIFT
name               Gearshift
magical_affinity   10
max_mana           20
armor_bonus        3
```

anotherWay.label: Why do keys get quotes?
anotherWay.text:
A box's name (a variable) never has quotes: `mana = 26`. A key inside a dictionary is a piece of text, so it does: `{"mana": 26}`.
Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label. *Box* here means a variable, like `mana = 26`. A key is never a box.

anotherWay.label: Keys and values in one big box
anotherWay.text:
The sheet is one big box. Inside, every value has its key:
```text
gearshift
+------------------------+
| "name"     "Gearshift" |
| "max_mana"          20 |
+------------------------+
```

anotherWay.label: A stat sheet
anotherWay.text: A stat sheet names every line: *armor bonus: 3*. You find a line by its name, not by counting lines. A dictionary works the same way.

1. `gearshift = {` opens the sheet.
2. Each line: a key in quotes, `:`, the value, `,`.
3. `}` closes the sheet.
At the Institute, each student had a record card: a tag and a value on every line. Mine said *talks too little*. Python keeps the same kind of card.

You've seen this. In the spell book part, `spell = {...}` held three keys: `"mana_cost"`, `"required_affinity"` and `"spell_function"`. Each key had quotes, a colon and a value. That was a dictionary.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text:
In math class, an input–output table has two columns. Each input appears once. A dictionary is like that: the keys are the left column, and the values are the right column.
```text
key          value
"name"       "Gearshift"
"max_mana"   20
```

Write one line for each key, like `"max_mana": 0,`, under `gearshift = {`.

1. Above `gearshift = {`, write Unit 3's recipe `max_mana_for(affinity)`. It hands back twice the affinity.
2. In the sheet, put `max_mana_for(10)` in place of the 20.
What's in it for me? Less math.

Write `def max_mana_for(affinity):` with `return affinity * 2` indented under it, above the sheet. Then change the max mana line to `"max_mana": max_mana_for(10),`.

campaignLink.why: You've seen this. In the spell book part, you filled in a dictionary like this one. Every key had quotes, a colon and a value. Now you know why the keys had quotes.

exercises.takeaway: A dictionary is curly braces `{ }` around `"key": value` lines, with commas. Keys are text, so they get quotes.

predict.explain: No quotes means look inside the box with this label. There is no box (variable) called `mana`, only a key inside `hero`, so Python stops with an error: *not defined*. With quotes, `hero["mana"]` reads the key: 26.

exercises.pairTalk: Pair talk: read your sheet to your partner, one line at a time: the key, then *colon*, then the value. Each of you types your own sheet.

exercises.title: Read by key
exercises.martu:
To read a value, write the sheet's name, then the key in square brackets: `gearshift["mana"]`. It's like looking up a word in a glossary: Python finds the key and hands you its value, 20. Read it as *gearshift, look up mana*.
The square brackets look like a list's. But a list wants a position number inside them, like `lucky[3]`. A dictionary wants a key, in quotes.
Line 9 has `Gearshift: 20 mana` typed in. Build that line from the sheet instead. Glue the pieces with `+`, as in Unit 1, and turn the number into text with `str()`. Then the line changes to match the sheet each time you press Run.

anotherWay.label: Sheet, then key
anotherWay.text:
```text
gearshift["mana"]
    |        |
  sheet     key -> 20
```
First the sheet's name, then the key in square brackets.

1. `gearshift["name"]` gives `"Gearshift"`.
2. `+ ": "` glues on a colon and a space.
3. `str(gearshift["mana"])` gives `"20"`.
4. `+ " mana"` glues on the last word.
Reading a key is like finding *armor bonus* on a stat sheet and reading across to its number. You look for the key, not the line number.
The sheet's name, then the key in square brackets: `gearshift["name"]`.

hints: Look at line 9: every part of `Gearshift: 20 mana` is typed in. Which two parts can you read from the sheet, and with which keys?
`shell["name"] + " has " + str(shell["ore"])` glues three pieces: a name read from the sheet, the text ` has `, and a number turned into text. `+` can glue a number only after `str()`.
Glue four pieces with `+`: `gearshift["name"]`, `": "`, `str(gearshift["mana"])` and `" mana"`. Or work in two steps, like the Example: `now = gearshift["mana"]` first, then glue `str(now)`.
Write `print(gearshift["name"] + ": " + str(gearshift["mana"]) + " mana")` in place of `print("Gearshift: 20 mana")`.

exercises.title: Key errors
exercises.martu:
A [[KeyError]] means the sheet has no key spelled exactly like the one you asked for. It's like a password: one wrong capital, and it doesn't work. Capitals count, and so do spaces: `"Max_Mana"` and `"max_mana"` are two different keys to Python.
When Python stops, read the box in the Console, in this order:
1. Read its title. It says what went wrong.
2. Read *Python's last line*. It names the key Python couldn't find, like `KeyError: 'Max_Mana'`. Python shows the key in `'` marks instead of `"`. Same text.
3. Find the line number. Fix that line: spell the key the way the sheet does.

anotherWay.label: How Python finds a key
anotherWay.text:
1. Python takes the key you wrote, letter by letter.
2. It looks for a key in the sheet spelled exactly the same.
3. If there is none, it stops with a `KeyError` and shows the key you wrote.

anotherWay.label: Two different keys
anotherWay.text:
```text
the sheet has:   "max_mana"
you wrote:       "Max_Mana"
                  ^   ^
          two capitals differ
```
A locker tagged *Max_Mana* and a locker tagged *max_mana* are two different lockers. Ask for one that isn't there, and you get nothing but an error.
KeyError: no key spelled exactly like that. Copy the key from the sheet.

exercises.title: Write by key
exercises.martu:
A sheet can change. Put the key on the left of `=`, and that key gets a new value. It's like a whiteboard: wipe the old number, write the new one. `shell["mana"] = 19` gives the key `"mana"` the value 19.
To cast a spell is to use it once, and it costs mana. Spending works like `mana = mana - 3` in Unit 1: `gearshift["mana"] = gearshift["mana"] - fire_bolt_cost`. Python works out the right side first, with what the sheet holds now: 20 − 6 is 14. Then the key `"mana"` gets 14, in place of the 20.
A key that isn't there yet? The same kind of line adds it: `shell["ore"] = "Velocite"`.

anotherWay.text:
1. Python reads `gearshift["mana"]` on the right: 20.
2. It takes away `fire_bolt_cost`: 20 - 6 is 14.
3. The key `"mana"` on the left gets 14.

anotherWay.label: Before and after
anotherWay.text:
```text
before:  "mana": 20
after:   "mana": 14
         "fuel": "starlode"
```
The same key, a new value. Then a new key.
Like a scoreboard: read the old score, work out the new one, and write it over the old one. The key stays; the number changes.
In Unit 1 you wrote `mana = mana - 3`. This is the same move, with a key in place of the box.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: In math class, m = m − 6 has no answer: no number is equal to itself minus 6. In Python, `=` isn't a math statement. Read it as *gets*: the key `"mana"` gets its old value minus the cost.

exercises.title: Is it in the book?
exercises.martu:
`in` asks a yes-or-no question: is this key in the dictionary? It's like checking a glossary for a word: you read the words, not their meanings. `"Glow" in spell_book` gives `True`. `in` looks at the keys only, never the values.
[[not in|`not in`]] asks the opposite: is it missing? Put it in an `if`, as in Unit 2, and the indented line runs only when the key is missing: `if "map" not in pack:`.
Try it if you like (it's not a step): after you press Run, change the `2` on line 6 to `3` and press Run again. Still `False`, yes? 3 is a value too, not a key.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? `in` checks keys
anotherWay.text: A dictionary is built to find keys fast. The values are what you get *after* you find a key. So `in` asks about keys and never looks at values: `2 in spell_book` is `False` even though 2 is Glow's cost.

anotherWay.label: Keys on the left
anotherWay.text:
`in` only reads the left side:
```text
  key            value
"Glow"       ->  2
"Warm Hands" ->  3
  ^ in looks here
```
Is Zelda on the class list? You read down the names, not the grades written next to them. The names are the keys.

exercises.title: A key from a box
exercises.martu:
A key can come from a variable. `spell_book[spell_name]` has no quotes, so Python opens the box `spell_name` first, finds `"Warm Hands"`, and then looks up that key. In English class, quotes mark a word talked about as a word: *"Lucky" has five letters*. Python's quotes work the same way.
`spell_book["spell_name"]` has quotes, so Python looks for a key spelled s-p-e-l-l-_-n-a-m-e, those exact letters. The book has no such key, so Python stops with a KeyError.
Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label.

anotherWay.label: What Python looks up
anotherWay.text:
`spell_book[spell_name]`:
1. No quotes: open the box `spell_name`. It holds `"Warm Hands"`.
2. Read the key `"Warm Hands"`: 3.
`spell_book["spell_name"]`:
1. Quotes: look for the key spelled `spell_name`.
2. There is none: KeyError.

predict.explain: With quotes, Python looks for a key spelled exactly `spell_name`. The book has no such key, so it stops with a KeyError. With no quotes, it opens the box first and finds `"Warm Hands"`.

exercises.title: Broken spell
exercises.martu:
Lucky's code has three [[bug|bugs]], all loud: each one makes Python stop with an error. Python shows one error at a time, so fix one, press Run again, and see what Python finds next. A new error is good news: Python got further.
When Python stops, read the box in the Console, in this order:
1. Read its title. It says what went wrong.
2. Read *Python's last line*. It says the same thing in Python's words.
3. Find the line number, and fix that line.
That's how everyone fixes code, yes?

anotherWay.label: One bug at a time
anotherWay.text:
1. Press Run. Read the box in the Console: its title, then Python's last line.
2. Find the line number. Fix that line.
3. Press Run again. A new error? Good: Python got further. That's the next bug.
4. No error? Your steps show what's left.

items.title: Why Does This Work? Keys and .get()
items.summary: Optional reading. Why each key appears only once, how `.get()` stops a KeyError, and why `in` is fast.
items.body:
Three things that make dictionaries work. Read them when you like. Nothing here is scored.
*Each key appears once.* A sheet has only one of each key, the way a glossary lists each word once. Give a key a value again, and the new value takes the old one's place, like a new number written over the old one on a whiteboard:
```python
hero = {"name": "Moth", "glug": 1}
hero["glug"] = 3
print(hero)
```
It prints `{'name': 'Moth', 'glug': 3}`. There is still only one `"glug"`. When Python shows a whole sheet, it uses `'` marks instead of `"`. Same text.
*A default instead of an error.* Reading a key that isn't there stops your code with a [[KeyError]]. [[.get()|`.get()`]] reads without stopping. `hero.get("glug", 0)` gives the value when the key is there, and the default, 0, when it isn't. A *default* is what you get when nothing else is there:
```python
hero = {"name": "Moth", "mana": 7}
print(hero.get("mana", 0))
print(hero.get("glug", 0))
```
It prints 7, then 0. No KeyError.
*Fast questions.* To find a value in a list, Python checks the items one by one, like opening a row of lockers. A dictionary works like the glossary at the back of a textbook: Python jumps straight to the key. So `"Glow" in spell_book` takes about the same time for 3 spells or 3,000.

exercises.title: Abilities inside
exercises.martu:
A value in a sheet can be a whole sheet too: a [[nested dictionary|sheet inside a sheet]]. Bomb Shell's key `"abilities"` holds a small sheet of his skills. To read one skill, use two keys in a row, outside first: `bomb_shell["abilities"]["dexterity"]` is 6. It's like a table of contents in English class: find the chapter first, then the section inside it. In Unit 4, `roster[3][1]` worked the same way: row first, then item.
`bomb_shell["abilities"]` on its own gives the whole inner sheet. English says it inside out, "the wisdom in Bomb Shell's abilities", but Python reads left to right, outside first.
Dexterity is how quick and careful a hero's hands are. Magical affinity is how strong a hero's magic is.

anotherWay.label: A sheet inside a sheet
anotherWay.text:
```text
bomb_shell
+---------------------------+
| "name" -> "Bomb Shell"    |
| "mana" -> 24              |
| "abilities" ->            |
|  +---------------------+  |
|  | "dexterity" -> 6    |  |
|  | "wisdom"    -> 8    |  |
|  | "magical_affinity"  |  |
|  |             -> 12   |  |
|  +---------------------+  |
+---------------------------+
```
The first key, `["abilities"]`, opens the small sheet inside. The second key, `["wisdom"]`, reads one value from it.

anotherWay.label: Left to right
anotherWay.text:
1. `bomb_shell` is the whole sheet.
2. `bomb_shell["abilities"]` is the inner sheet: `{'dexterity': 6, 'wisdom': 8, ...}`.
3. `bomb_shell["abilities"]["wisdom"]` is one value from that inner sheet: 8.
Each pair of square brackets goes one level in.

anotherWay.text: When you held the barrier in the campaign, the code read `caster["abilities"]["magical_affinity"]`: the caster's sheet, then the `"abilities"` sheet inside it, then one value. The same two keys in a row.
At the Institute, each student's record had a pocket on the back with a smaller card of scores. To read a score, you opened the record, then the pocket. The score was never on the front page.

exercises.title: Change inside
exercises.martu:
To change a value inside a sheet, put the same two keys on the left of `=`. It's the Unit 1 move, `mana = mana - spell_cost`: Python works out the right side first, with the old value, then puts the answer back in the same spot.
Do it in three moves: *get it, change it, put it back.* In the Example, `old = jar["lid"]["turns"]` gets the old number, 4. Then `jar["lid"]["turns"] = old + 1` works out 5 and puts it back, with the same two keys on the left.
Dexterity is how quick and careful a hero's hands are.

anotherWay.label: Get it, change it, put it back
anotherWay.text:
1. Get it: `dex = bomb_shell["abilities"]["dexterity"]` puts 6 in `dex`.
2. Change it: `dex + 2` is 8.
3. Put it back: `bomb_shell["abilities"]["dexterity"] = dex + 2` stores 8 in the same spot, inside `"abilities"`.
The wisdom next to it does not change.

anotherWay.label: Same keys, both lines
anotherWay.text:
```text
get it:       6 -> dex
change it:    dex + 2 is 8
put it back:  8 -> ["abilities"]
                   ["dexterity"]
```
The first line and the last line use the same two keys. The first line reads the old value. The last line writes the new value.
A score sheet in a binder: find the page, find the line, read the number, erase it, and write the new number on the same line. You don't start a new sheet.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: When you held the barrier, the campaign's code wrote `caster["mana"] = caster["mana"] - spell["mana_cost"]`. It read the old value, changed it, and put it back. Here the value sits one level deeper, so each side has two keys.

anotherWay.label: In one line
anotherWay.text: You can also do it in one line, like the campaign: `caster["mana"] = caster["mana"] - cost`, with the same keys on both sides of `=`. Both ways pass the step.

exercises.title: The roster
exercises.martu:
A roster is a list of everyone on a team. Here `roster` is a [[list of dictionaries|list of sheets]], one per hero. To read one value, give the position first, then the key: `roster[1]["name"]` is `Gearshift`. It's like a class roster in a table: pick the row by its number, then the column by its name. Positions count from 0, like a ruler, so `roster[1]` is the second sheet.
The list remembers the order. Each sheet remembers what its values mean.
A hero's name is not a position. `roster["Lucky"]` stops Python with an error, because a list only takes whole numbers in its square brackets.

anotherWay.label: A row of sheets
anotherWay.text:
```text
roster
  [0]  oogrish
  [1]  gearshift
  [2]  bomb_shell
  [3]  lucky

roster[2]["name"]
  [2]      -> the bomb_shell sheet
  ["name"] -> "Bomb Shell"
```
The list numbers its sheets from 0. Each sheet inside it has its own keys.

1. `roster[0]`: the first sheet, Oogrish's.
2. `["abilities"]`: his `"abilities"` sheet.
3. `["intelligence"]`: one value from that sheet, 17.
Position numbers for the list. Keys in quotes for the sheets.

exercises.title: A spell book of spells
exercises.martu:
A spell book is a sheet of spells. Each key is a spell's name, and each value is a small sheet: what the spell costs, and the affinity it needs. To add a page, store the spell under its name: `spell_book[spell_name] = spell`. You did this in Stat Sheets. With no quotes, Python looks inside `spell_name` and finds `"Lantern Ward"`.
Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label. With quotes, `spell_book["spell_name"]` would make a page called spell_name, the way quotation marks in English class can mean the word itself.
Then ask first, the way the campaign did: `if spell_name not in spell_book:`, with the store line indented under it. A page that is already there stays as it is.

anotherWay.label: A book of pages
anotherWay.text:
```text
spell_book
  "Glow"         -> {cost 2,
                     need 3}
  "Lantern Ward" -> {cost 6,
                     need 9}
```
`spell_name` holds the page's name. `spell` holds what goes on the page.

1. `spell_name` holds `"Lantern Ward"`.
2. `spell_book[spell_name]`: Python looks inside the box `spell_name` and finds `"Lantern Ward"`.
3. `= spell` stores the whole spell sheet on that page.
4. Glow's page is still there.
5. `if spell_name not in spell_book:` asks first, so a name that already has a page keeps it.

anotherWay.label: From English class
anotherWay.text: In English, quotation marks can mean the word itself: "Lucky" has five letters. Python works the same way. `spell_book["spell_name"]` means a page called those exact letters. `spell_book[spell_name]` means the name the variable holds, `"Lantern Ward"`.

exercises.title: Can they cast?
exercises.martu:
This is the campaign's barrier code, in three moves: get it, compare, act. *Get it:* read a value out of its sheet, through every key on the way. *Compare:* use `<` to ask if it's lower than what the spell needs. Your code's notes call it a test. *Act:* warn, or cast the spell. It's Unit 2's `if` / `elif` / `else`, like a grading scale: Python checks from the top and stops at the first question whose answer is True.
The game hands you `caster`. Magical affinity is how strong a hero's magic is:
```text
caster (from the game)
  "name"      -> "Bomb Shell"
  "mana"      -> 24
  "abilities" ->
    "magical_affinity" -> 12
```
One rule from the campaign: exactly enough still casts. On a number line, `<` is an open dot, so 9 is not lower than 9.

anotherWay.label: Get it, compare, act
anotherWay.text:
1. Get it: `caster["abilities"]["magical_affinity"]` is 12. `spell["required_affinity"]` is 9.
2. Compare: is 12 lower than 9? No, so Python skips `print("Not skilled enough.")`.
3. Get it: `caster["mana"]` is 24. `spell["mana_cost"]` is 6. Is 24 lower than 6? No.
4. Act: the `else`. 24 - 6 is 18. Print 18.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: The `hold-the-barrier` comments said: if the affinity is lower than the spell's required affinity, say they aren't skilled enough. Otherwise, if the mana is lower than the cost, say so. Otherwise, cast and subtract. This is that chain, with `print` in place of `print_prompt`.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: On a number line, `<` is an open dot. `affinity < 9` is True for 8, 7, 6 and lower, but not for 9 itself. That's why exactly enough still casts. `<=` would be a filled dot, and it would turn away a caster with exactly 9.

anotherWay.label: Three doors
anotherWay.text:
```text
affinity too low? -yes-> Not skilled
      | no
mana too low? ---yes---> Needs mana
      | no
else: spend, print the mana
```
Python takes the first door that opens, and only that one.

exercises.title: Broken spell
exercises.martu:
This program has three mistakes, one per line. Python stops at the first one. Read the error box in the Console like a teacher's note in the margin. Its title says what went wrong. Python's last line says it in Python's words. The line number says which line to fix.
A KeyError means the sheet has no key spelled like that on that level. A TypeError about list indices means a list got a name instead of a position. A NameError means a word that needs quotes has none.
Fix one line, press Run again, and Python shows you the next mistake. That's normal: a new error means Python got further.

anotherWay.label: One mistake at a time
anotherWay.text:
1. Press Run. Read the box in the Console: its title, then Python's last line.
2. Find the line number in the box, and fix that line.
3. Press Run again. A new error? Good: Python got further. That's the next mistake.
4. No error? Your steps show what is left.

anotherWay.label: What each error means
anotherWay.text:
```text
KeyError: 'dexterity'
  no key spelled like that
  here: look one level in
TypeError: list indices...
  a list got a name
  use a position number
NameError: name 'Glow'
  a word with no quotes
  add the quotes
```
Inner keys need the outer key first. Lists take position numbers. Keys are text, so they take quotes.

items.title: Dictionaries Quiz
items.summary: Eight questions on keys, sheets inside sheets, rosters and spell books. Retake it as often as you like.

questions.explain: `in` looks at the keys only, letter for letter, like looking up words in a glossary, never the definitions. The key is `"Glow"` with a capital G, so `"glow"` is not a key: `False`. 2 is a value, not a key, so `2 in pack` is `False` too.

questions.q: `spell_name` holds `"Glow"`. Which line prints Glow's cost?

whyWrong.0: With quotes, Python looks for a key spelled s-p-e-l-l-_-n-a-m-e. The book has no such key, so it stops with a KeyError.
whyWrong.2: A sheet is read with square brackets, not a dot. A dot is for tools like `.lower()`, and a sheet has no tool called `spell_name`, so Python stops with an error.

questions.explain: No quotes means look inside the box: `spell_name` holds `"Glow"`, so `spell_book[spell_name]` reads Glow's page, 2.

questions.q: Put the lines in order, with their indents. Build the spell from `cost` and `needed`, then store it under the name in `spell_name`.
questions.explain: Python reads top to bottom, so make the variables first, then the spell that uses them, then store it. `spell_book[spell_name]` has no quotes, so the page is called Frost Veil. With quotes, it would be called spell_name.
Outer key, then inner key. `hero["abilities"]` is Lucky's inner sheet. `["strength"]` reads one value from it: 17. One key alone would print the whole inner sheet.

questions.q: Fill the blank so the hero pays `cost` from their mana. The program should print 18.
questions.explain: Python works out the right side first: the old mana, 24, minus `cost`, 6, is 18. Then the key `"mana"` on the left gets 18. It's Unit 1's `mana = mana - spell_cost`, with a key.

questions.q: This program stops with `KeyError: 'wisdom'`. Fix it so it prints Lucky's wisdom.
questions.explain: Wisdom is not on the big sheet. It lives inside `"abilities"`, so the read needs the outer key first: `hero["abilities"]["wisdom"]`.
`roster[1]` is the second sheet, Lucky's, because positions count from 0. Then `["mana"]` reads his mana: 26.
During the call, `book` holds the spell book and `name` holds `"Glow"`, the way x in f(x) gets a number. `book[name]` has no quotes, so it looks inside `name`, reads Glow's page and hands back 2.

items.title: Mar'tu's Ledger of Heroes
items.summary: Make a sheet for every hero, work out their mana with a recipe, and put all four sheets in a roster.
items.intro:
Mar'tu keeps a ledger, a record book, with one sheet per hero. Every sheet uses the same keys, so any sheet can be read the same way.
There are three parts, in order, and the notes `# A.`, `# B.` and `# C.` in your code mark them: A. the sheets, B. a recipe that works out each hero's mana, and C. the roster, a list of all four sheets.
Use the party table. INT is intelligence, WIS is wisdom, DEX is dexterity, STR is strength, and AFF is magical affinity:
```text
hero        INT WIS DEX STR AFF
Oogrish      17  17  14  13   9
Gearshift    14  15  13  17  10
Bomb Shell   14   8   6  15  12
Lucky        13  12  15  17  13
```
The keys are `"intelligence"`, `"wisdom"`, `"dexterity"`, `"strength"` and `"magical_affinity"`. Oogrish and Bomb Shell are done for you. For Gearshift and Lucky, use `"magical_affinity"` and pick two more abilities each.
items.martu:
A ledger is a record book. In mine, every hero's sheet has the same keys, the way every row of a table in math class has the same columns. Then the same kind of line reads any hero: `oogrish["abilities"]["wisdom"]` is 17, and the same keys work on any sheet that has a wisdom.
I test your code with other affinities, like testing a formula in math class with other numbers. So every max mana has to come from your recipe and the sheet, never a number you typed. My tests don't change your code.
At the Institute, every record had the same keys in the same places. A record nobody can read is a diary, yes?

```text
  "spell_book" -> {}
  "max_mana"   -> 20  (task 3)
  "mana"       -> 20  (task 3)
```

items.title: The Barrier, From Blank
items.summary: Write the whole `cast_spell` recipe from a blank page, the way the campaign's barrier worked.
items.martu:
Write the campaign's barrier recipe, `cast_spell(caster, spell_name)`, from a blank page. You know every piece: `not in`, two keys in a row, `if` / `elif` / `else`, and a change by key. Work from this outline, as in English class. Each point becomes a few lines, and the indents show where each line belongs:
1. If the name is not in the caster's `"spell_book"`, print a message.
2. Otherwise, read the spell from the book.
3. If the affinity is lower than the spell's `"required_affinity"`, say they're not skilled enough.
4. Otherwise, if the mana is lower than its `"mana_cost"`, say they need more mana.
5. Otherwise, subtract the cost from `caster["mana"]`.
Like the campaign's recipe, yours changes the sheet it's handed. I test it with other casters.

anotherWay.label: The campaign's order
anotherWay.text:
1. Ask the book: `not in` first.
2. Read the spell: the book, by the name.
3. Compare the affinity: `<`.
4. `elif`: compare the mana.
5. `else`: take the cost from the mana, by key.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: In `hold-the-barrier`, the game gave you this recipe with its `not in` question already written, and you filled in the chain. The campaign's recipe stopped after the message with `return`. Here, an `else` does the same job. In Sheets Inside Sheets, Can they cast? was this chain on its own.

anotherWay.label: Doors in doors
anotherWay.text:
```text
name not in book? --> message
  else: read the spell
    affinity low? --> not skilled
    mana low? -----> more mana
    else: spend the cost
```
Python takes the first door that opens, and only that one.

exercises.title: Twin: spend by key
exercises.martu:
This is a twin of Write by key, in Stat Sheets: the same move, on another sheet. To spend mana by key, read the old mana, take away the cost, and put the answer back under the same key. It's the whiteboard from Write by key: read the old number, wipe it, write the new one. In the Example, `jar["oil"] = jar["oil"] - spill` works out 9 − 2 and puts 7 back under `"oil"`.
It's Unit 1's `mana = mana - spell_cost`, with a key in place of the box. A *ward* is a spell that protects, and casting it once costs `ward_cost`.

anotherWay.text:
1. Python works out the right side first: `oogrish["mana"]` is 18 and `ward_cost` is 5, so 18 − 5 is 13.
2. Then the left side: 13 goes back under the key `"mana"`, in place of the 18.
3. `print(oogrish["mana"])` shows 13.

exercises.title: Twin: store by name
exercises.martu:
This is a twin of A spell book of spells: another page for another book. `book[spell_name] = spell` stores the spell under the name that `spell_name` holds. It's like the glossary at the back of a textbook: the word is the key, and what it means is the value. In the Example, `shelf[title] = 12` makes a page called Runes, because `title` holds `"Runes"`.
Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label. With quotes, `book["spell_name"]` would make a page called spell_name.
Then ask the book whether it has that key: `spell_name in book` shows `True` or `False`. `in` looks only at the keys, never the values.

exercises.title: Make a sheet
exercises.martu:
Mar'tu's notes so far: Gearshift's tank holds starlode, his fuel. Lantern Ward is in the spell book. The barrier holds again. Now make Lucky's sheet, a [[dictionary]], from this card:

```text
LUCKY
name              Lucky
```

exercises.title: A value inside a sheet
exercises.martu:
Gearshift's sheet has an inner sheet: `"abilities"` is a smaller sheet inside the big one. The `# 2.` note calls it the card. First, print Gearshift's wisdom, read from the sheet. Then Gearshift trains, so add 2 to the wisdom inside `"abilities"`. I test your code with another wisdom, so read it from the sheet. Don't type it.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to the lesson Sheets Inside Sheets. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

anotherWay.label: A sheet inside a sheet
anotherWay.text:
```text
gearshift
  "name"
  "mana"
  "abilities"
      "wisdom"
```
The outer key, `"abilities"`, gives the inner sheet. The inner key gives one value from it. To change that value, use the same two keys on the left of `=`.

1. `gearshift["abilities"]` is the whole inner sheet.
2. One more key in square brackets reads one value from that inner sheet.
3. Put the read inside `print(...)`.
4. To change it, put the old value in a variable. Then put the new value back, with the same two keys on the left of `=`.

exercises.title: Store a spell by name
exercises.martu:
`book` is a book of spells: a sheet with one page for each spell, and each page's key is the spell's name. First, make the new spell from `cost`, its price in mana, and `needed`, how strong a caster's magic must be. Then store it in `book`, with the name in `spell_name` as the key. Store it only if that name is not in `book` yet, so a page that is already there stays as it is. I test your code with other names and numbers.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to the lesson Sheets Inside Sheets. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

anotherWay.text:
1. Make `spell`: two keys in quotes, each with a variable as its value. The variables get no quotes.
2. Ask the book: is the name in `spell_name` missing from `book`?
3. If it is, store the spell under that name, on a line indented under the `if`. No quotes go around `spell_name`.

This code stops with a [[KeyError]]: Python can't find a key it was asked for. Read the box in the Console: first its title, then *Python's last line*. Find the line number it gives, and fix the read on that line so the code runs. Leave the sheet as it is.
Then finish the `if` / `elif` / `else` chain: replace `False` with a question about the caster's mana and `cost`. I test your code with other casters and costs.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to the lesson Sheets Inside Sheets. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

anotherWay.text:
1. Read the box in the Console. *Python's last line* gives the key Python couldn't find.
2. Find that key in the sheet: is it on the big sheet, or inside `"abilities"`?
3. Read the outer key first, then the inner key.
4. In the `elif`, compare the caster's mana with `cost`. *Lower than* is `<`.

anotherWay.label: Where the keys live
anotherWay.text:
```text
caster
  "name"
  "mana"
  "abilities"
      "magical_affinity"
```
The affinity is one level down, inside `"abilities"`. The mana is on the big sheet.

exercises.title: A roster of sheets
exercises.martu:
`roster` is a list of four sheets, one for each hero. First, print the name of the hero at position 1 in `roster`. Then that hero casts a spell, which costs mana: take `cost` away from their mana, using `roster` to reach their sheet. I test your code with other numbers, and with the heroes in another order.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to the lesson Sheets Inside Sheets. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

anotherWay.label: A row of sheets
anotherWay.text:
```text
roster
  [0]  oogrish
  [1]  gearshift
  [2]  bomb_shell
  [3]  lucky
```
Positions in the list count from 0. Each sheet inside it has a key on every value.

1. `roster[1]` is one whole sheet.
2. Then a key reads one value from it.
3. To spend, read the old mana on the right of `=`, take `cost` away, and store the answer under the same key, on the left.

items.title: Quick Check 5 · Form A questions
items.summary: Three questions that go with Quick Check 5. To pass the Quick Check, get 2 of the 3 right.

questions.explain: `in` looks at the keys only, like looking for a word in a glossary, never at its meaning. `"Spark"` is a key, so the first line shows `True`. `"Glow"` is not a key, so `not in` shows `True`. 4 is a value, not a key, so `4 in book` is `False`.

questions.q: Which of these sheets can Python read without an error?

whyWrong.0: With no quotes, Python reads `name` as a box's name. It looks for a box called `name`, finds none, and stops with a NameError. Keys are text, so they need quotes.
whyWrong.1: `=` puts a value in a box. Inside a sheet, Python stops with an error at the `=`, because a colon goes between each key and its value.
whyWrong.3: A comma is missing after `"Pell"`, so Python can't read the sheet and stops with an error: invalid syntax.

questions.explain: Keys are text, so each one gets quotes. A colon goes between a key and its value, like a word and its meaning in a glossary, and a comma goes between one pair and the next. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label.

No quotes means look inside the box: `spell_name` holds `"Spark"`, so Python reads the page for Spark, 5. With quotes, `book["spell_name"]` would look for a page called spell_name and stop with a KeyError.

exercises.title: Make a sheet
exercises.martu:
Mar'tu's notes so far: Gearshift's tank holds starlode, his fuel. Lantern Ward is in the spell book. The barrier holds again. Now make Bomb Shell's sheet, a [[dictionary]], from this card:
```text
BOMB SHELL
name              Bomb Shell
magical_affinity  12
max_mana          24
armor_bonus       3
```
On the card, each key is on the left and its value is on the right. Use all four keys, and copy each one letter for letter.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to the lesson Stat Sheets. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

anotherWay.text:
1. `bomb_shell = {` opens the sheet.
2. Write one line for each key on the card: the key in quotes, then `:`, then the value, then `,`.
3. `}` closes the sheet.

anotherWay.label: Why do keys get quotes?
anotherWay.text: A box's name (a variable) never has quotes: `mana = 26`. A key is text inside the sheet, like a word you look up in a glossary, so it gets quotes: `{"mana": 26}`. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label.

Then Oogrish trains, so add 2 to the wisdom inside `"abilities"`. I test your code with another wisdom, so read it from the sheet. Don't type it.

anotherWay.label: A sheet inside a sheet
anotherWay.text:
```text
oogrish
  "name"
  "mana"
  "abilities"
      "wisdom"
```
The outer key, `"abilities"`, gives the inner sheet. The inner key gives one value from it. To change that value, use the same two keys on the left of `=`.

1. `oogrish["abilities"]` is the whole inner sheet.
2. One more key in square brackets reads one value from that inner sheet.
3. Put the read inside `print(...)`.
4. To change it, put the old value in a variable. Then put the new value back, with the same two keys on the left of `=`.

exercises.title: Store a spell by name
exercises.martu:
`wards` is a book of spells: a sheet with one page for each spell, and each page's key is the spell's name. A *ward* is a spell that protects. First, make the new spell from `cost`, its price in mana, and `needed`, how strong a caster's magic must be. Then store it in `wards`, with the name in `ward_name` as the key. Store it only if that name is not in `wards` yet, so a page that is already there stays as it is. I test your code with other names and numbers.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to the lesson Sheets Inside Sheets. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

items.title: Quick Check 5 · Form B questions
items.summary: Three questions that go with Quick Check 5. To pass the Quick Check, get 2 of the 3 right.

questions.explain: `in` looks at the keys only, like looking for a word in a glossary, never at its meaning. `"Iron Bark"` is a key, so the first line shows `True`. `"Stone Skin"` is a key too, so `not in` shows `False`. 6 is a value, not a key, so `6 in wards` is `False`.

questions.q: Which of these sheets can Python read without an error?

whyWrong.1: With no quotes, Python reads `name` as a box's name. It looks for a box called `name`, finds none, and stops with a NameError. Keys are text, so they need quotes.
whyWrong.2: `=` puts a value in a box. Inside a sheet, Python stops with an error at the `=`, because a colon goes between each key and its value.
whyWrong.3: A colon is missing after `"name"`, so Python can't read the sheet and stops with an error: invalid syntax.

questions.explain: Keys are text, so each one gets quotes. A colon goes between a key and its value, like a word and its meaning in a glossary, and a comma goes between one pair and the next. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label.

No quotes means look inside the box: `ward_name` holds `"Stone Skin"`, so Python reads the page for Stone Skin, 4. With quotes, `wards["ward_name"]` would look for a page called ward_name and stop with a KeyError.

items.title: Mar'tu's Chalk Notes: Dictionaries
items.summary: Every idea from Unit 5 on one page, with a short example of each. You can print it.

entries.note: Curly braces `{ }` hold the sheet (a dictionary). Each line is a key in quotes, a colon, its value and a comma. It works like a glossary: you look up the word (the key) to find its meaning (the value). (Lesson: Stat Sheets)

entries.concept: Box names have no quotes. Keys do.
entries.note: A box's name (a variable) never has quotes. A key is text inside the sheet, so it does. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label.
Square brackets `[ ]` with a key in quotes inside read one value. Read `hero["name"]` as *hero, look up name*.

Python works out the right side first: the old mana, 26, minus 3 is 23. Then it stores 23 under the same key, like a new number written over the old one on a whiteboard. You've seen this: `caster["mana"] = caster["mana"] - spell["mana_cost"]`.
If the sheet doesn't have the key yet, `=` adds it. If it does, `=` changes its value. A key is never there twice.
`in` asks a yes-or-no question about the keys only. 2 is a value, not a key, so `2 in book` is `False`. You've seen this: `if spell_name not in caster["spell_book"]:`.
No quotes: Python looks inside `spell_name` and finds `"Warm Hands"`. `book["spell_name"]`, with quotes, looks for a key spelled s-p-e-l-l-_-n-a-m-e, and stops with a KeyError.

Outer key first, then inner key, like a table of contents: chapter, then section. One key alone gives the whole inner sheet. You've seen this: `caster["abilities"]["magical_affinity"]`. (Lesson: Sheets Inside Sheets)

entries.concept: Change a value inside a sheet
entries.note: Get it, change it, put it back. `w` gets the old wisdom, 8. The next line puts the new one, 11, back in the same spot, with the same two keys on the left of `=`.
Position first, counting from 0, then the key. The list remembers the order, and each sheet remembers what its values mean. In the campaign, a list like this was `party.members`.
The key comes from the variable `name`, so the page is called Warm Hands. You've seen this: `spell_book[spell_name] = spell`.

entries.concept: Store only when it is new
entries.note: `not in` asks first, so a page that is already there stays as it is. The store line is indented under the `if`, so it runs only when the name is new.

Get it: read the value through every key. Compare: `<` asks *lower than*, so exactly enough still casts. Act: only one part of the chain runs, the first one whose question is `True`. You've seen this when you held the barrier.

entries.concept: (extra) `.get()`: a backup value, not an error
entries.note: `hero.get("glug", 0)` gives the value of `"glug"`, or 0 when the sheet has no such key, in place of a KeyError. (Article: Why Does This Work? Keys and .get())

entries.concept: Error: a key with no quotes
entries.note: NameError: name 'name' is not defined. With no quotes, Python reads `name` as a box's name, and there is no such box. Keys are text, so they get quotes: `"name"`.
SyntaxError: cannot assign to literal here. Maybe you meant '==' instead of '='? Python's guess is wrong here: inside a sheet, a colon goes between a key and its value.
SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Perhaps you forgot a comma? After a number, Python gives that line's number. After text, it gives the next line, so check the line above it too.
SyntaxError: ':' expected after dictionary key. Every key needs a colon before its value.
KeyError: 'Mana'. No key is spelled exactly like that. Check the spelling, the capitals and the spaces.
KeyError: 'wisdom'. `"wisdom"` is inside the inner sheet `"abilities"`, so read the outer key first: `hero["abilities"]["wisdom"]`.

entries.concept: Error: a dot, not square brackets
entries.note: AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'mana'. Read a sheet with square brackets `[ ]` and the key in quotes: `hero["mana"]`.
TypeError: 'dict' object is not callable. Parentheses `( )` call a recipe. A sheet takes square brackets `[ ]`: `hero["mana"]`.

entries.concept: Error: a position on a sheet
entries.note: KeyError: 0. A sheet has no positions, only keys.

entries.concept: Error: a name as a list position
entries.note: TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str. A list takes a position number, counting from 0: `roster[0]`.

entries.concept: Error: a variable's name in quotes
entries.note: KeyError: 'spell_name'. With quotes, Python looks for those exact letters. Without them, it looks inside the variable.
